pages.title: Van Allen Building
pages.text:
The Van Allen Building, also known as Van Allen and Company Department Store, is a historic building at the northwest corner of Fifth Avenue South and Second Street in Clinton, Iowa, United States. The four-story building was designed by Louis Sullivan and commissioned by John Delbert Van Allen. Constructed between 1913 and 1914 as a department store, it has since been converted into an apartment building with commercial space. The Van Allen Building was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1976 for its architecture.
Unlike Sullivan's earlier work, the design includes some purely decorative elements, and the interior arrangement influenced the design of the facade. The ground floor has storefront windows and entrances, while the upper stories have a brick facade with terracotta decorations such as three decorative mullions. The building has a steel frame, which divides the interior spaces into aisles, alongside mechanical features such as pneumatic tube and forced-air systems. The structure spans 45,000 square feet (4,200 m2) and originally had store departments on each floor, along with a balcony above the first floor. The modern apartment building has retail on the ground floor, 19 apartments on the upper stories, and an atrium. Over the years, the building's design has received mixed commentary.
Van Allen took over an existing store on the site in 1892 and, after a series of expansions, began planning a new store building in 1910. Following a recommendation from another of Sullivan's clients in Iowa, Van Allen hired Sullivan the next year. The store opened in September 1914 and was remodeled several times over the next half-century. Petersen-Harned-Von Maur took over the store in 1968 and operated it until its closure in 1987. Afterward, Crombie Taylor led efforts to restore the building, which partially reopened in 1991. Following unsuccessful attempts to find some other use for the building, Heartland Properties and Community Housing Initiatives converted it to housing between 2001 and 2003.


== Site ==
The Van Allen Building is located at the northwest corner of Fifth Avenue South and Second Street in Clinton, Iowa, United States. Second Street runs north–south along the lot's eastern boundary, and Fifth Avenue South runs west–east at the southern boundary. As built, the structure occupied a site with frontage of 86 feet (26 m) on Fifth Avenue South and 90 feet (27 m) on Second Street. The westernmost bay measures 22 feet (6.7 m) wide and extends 140 feet (43 m) north–south, creating an annex extending north from the lot's northwestern corner. The maximum dimensions of the lot are thus 86 by 140 feet (26 by 43 m).
Before the building was constructed in the 1910s, the intersection of Fifth Avenue South and Second Street had been the commercial center of the small town of Clinton, since it was near the banks of the Mississippi River. The corner contained the Young Block, which had a mercantile store, grocer, photographer, blacksmith, hotel, and clubhouse. The building's first occupant, Van Allen & Son Company, had occupied an earlier structure on the same site. Several blocks to the south are the Clinton Railroad Bridge (which was completed in 1909, just before the building was erected) and the Gateway Bridge for road traffic. When the current building was constructed, the company's founder, John Delbert Van Allen, had proposed installing elaborate electroliers on Fifth Avenue South to complement the building's construction.


== Architecture ==
The Van Allen Building was designed for the John D. Van Allen & Son Company by Louis Sullivan as a four-story, steel framed building. The design shares significant design features with Sullivan's previous designs for early skyscrapers. In particular, the steel frame is similar to Sullivan's high-rise designs, and the articulation (or arrangement) of the facade is a scaled-down version of the articulation used in Sullivan's earlier Carson Pirie Scott Store in Chicago. In contrast to other structures, the exterior was designed only after the interior details had been laid out. John B. Van Allen—the grandson of the original proprietor, John D. Van Allen—said that Sullivan's design had been forward-looking even when it was built in 1913, incorporating features such as space for a second elevator shaft. The steel frame was intended to accommodate three extra stories (for a total of seven) if the need arose.
Sullivan designed the building immediately after finishing St. Paul United Methodist Church in Cedar Rapids, Iowa; at the time, he was in the midst of designing his jewel box banks in the Midwest. The Van Allen commission was one of five commissions Sullivan received in Iowa. It came after the Peoples Savings Bank and St. Paul's Church in Cedar Rapids, and before the Henry Adams Building in Algona and the Merchants' National Bank in Grinnell. It was the only department store Sullivan designed for a smaller city. 


=== Facade ===
Since the Van Allen Building was relatively short and wide, Sullivan articulated it horizontally, with horizontal spandrel panels and wide windows. The facade is divided into five bays on its eastern elevation and three on its southern elevation, the latter corresponding to the aisles inside.  On the southern elevation, the bays are asymmetrical (gradually widening from west to east) to avoid a neighboring property on the western end, and to accommodate the depth of Second Street's storefront displays on the eastern end. Similarly, because of the storefront displays on Fifth Avenue South, the eastern elevation's southernmost (left) bay is wider than the others.
In contrast to Sullivan's earlier work, which tended toward a more functional "form follows function" philosophy, the Van Allen Building has decorative elements that do not serve any structural purpose. Terracotta trim is used throughout the facade.  Kristian Schneider, a craftsman who had collaborated with Sullivan on several previous projects, executed the decorations for the Van Allen Building.


==== Ground story ====

At ground level, the building was constructed with a main entrance on Fifth Avenue South, a side door on Second Street, and a third entrance for patrons of the haberdashery. The haberdasher's entrance was designed in a nondescript manner, to allow men to visit the haberdashery without drawing attention. It is no longer extant, having been removed in 1940. Also at ground level are a pair of plaques containing the family's name and coat of arms.
The rest of the ground story contains storefront windows with ornamental iron frames, separated by projecting green-marble piers. The bottom edges of the storefront windows are built very close to the sidewalks, to increase visibility of objects inside, and are placed on ornamental iron sills. The windows were covered by overhanging awnings. Behind the storefront windows were display areas with mirrored side walls and mahogany rear walls. Other decorative details on the facade include a nameplate denoting the Van Allen family, and the family crest.


==== Upper stories ====
The upper facade uses over half a million bricks, which are mottled and vary in color because of the presence of mineral spots, which create imperfections. The brick is variously described as being soft brown, sandy, grayish brown, or gray with a purple tint. The tone is characterized as evoking the sediment on the Mississippi River's banks or the color of Iowa's soil. The upper stories' brickwork is smooth, and the joints between different bricks are flush, except in piers separating each window. This specific type of brick was made locally by the Price Brick Yard; it was not reused in Sullivan's other work, though similar bricks were used in the nearby Orpheum Theatre. There are steel columns behind all of the piers, except the southernmost pier on the eastern elevation, which was included solely for esthetic purposes.
The southern elevation has three slender mullions, which are made of terracotta and rise three stories. The mullions protrude from the facade, similarly to the extruded I-beams of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe's mid-20th-century work. The presence of the mullions were variously cited as creating a monumental feeling, concealing the asymmetrical bays, accenting the building's height, or drawing attention to the use of long-span girders inside. The bottoms of each mullion rest on corbels containing inscriptions that read "VA", the initials of the Van Allen family. Atop the mullions are medallions with foliate ornament, including green corbels and finials. The color of the ornament was intended to evoke leaves and branches. Behind the medallions are blue-and-white tiled panels. The panels, a purely esthetic element, allude to the Dutch heritage of Van Allen. Drawings show that, had the building been expanded to seven stories, the exterior mullions may also have been extended. The Second Street elevation does not contain mullions.
Both the southern and eastern elevations have six windows on each floor, rather than conforming to the three-by-five-bay interior layout. The mullions and piers divide the southern windows in a 1-2-2-1 pattern, creating what the historians William Jordy and William Pierson Jr. described as "ambiguity of the fenestration". The eastern elevation's windows are divided only by the piers. Sullivan de-emphasized the windows themselves from the design, a contrast to the Carson's building, where the windows were accented. Each window opening on the upper stories consists of a large plate-glass pane, with a smaller sash window next to it. On the southern elevation, the sash windows are placed next to the nearest mullions. The large windows allowed views of the Mississippi River from inside, and their width was intended to allude to the use of a steel frame inside.
Horizontal terracotta courses run beneath and above each window, respectively connecting the windowsills and lintels of each story's windows. Unlike the brick, the terracotta is not mottled, though it does have a brown tint. Different designs were used for the courses above the first story; the lintels above the second, third, and fourth stories; and the frieze just below the top of the roof's parapet. The roofline, 64+3⁄4 feet (19.7 m) above street level, has a slight, protruding cornice.


=== Structural and mechanical features ===
The columns are spaced 28 feet (8.5 m) apart, roughly corresponding to the three bays on the southern elevation, and are connected by long-span girders running east–west. Sullivan contemplated using intermediate columns on the upper floors, but structural engineers Ritter & Mott advised him that the long girders could be used on all floors. The beams themselves are encased in concrete. Timber joists, which were intended to burn at a slower rate during fires, were installed under the hardwood floor, connecting the primary steel girders. An elevator and stairs, connecting the four above-ground stories, were placed on the northern side of the building. Two stairs descended to the basement. Sullivan left provisions for a second elevator shaft in case additional stories were built.
To reduce the risk of fire, Sullivan used self-closing fire doors for stairways. Red exit sign lamps were lit with electricity and gas, an innovation for the time. There were also sprinklers on the ceiling, supplied by a water tank on the roof. The basement had two boilers, along with a coal room and an ash room. The basement also contained a pneumatic tube system for cashiers. A forced-air system cleaned and heated air, which was pumped through the first floor and basement; the system could completely refresh the air in the basement within eight minutes, and on the upper floors within fifteen minutes. The air filtration system was similar to that used in Sullivan's jewel box banks, such as the People's Federal Savings and Loan Association (1918) in Sidney, Ohio. On upper stories, there was originally no mechanical ventilation, and breezes instead came in through the windows. Utility pipes and electric ducts were bundled within a single shaft, and drinking fountains were added on each floor. The basement also had a pump system that could be used during floods.


=== Interior ===

Inside, the building spans 45,000 square feet (4,200 m2); including basement spaces, it covers more than 50,000 square feet (4,600 m2). The interior originally had mahogany woodwork and illuminated display cabinets. The arrangement of the departments dictated the interior layout, with the most profitable departments clustered on the ground floor, which had the highest ceiling. The ground floor was originally for general dry goods and menswear, including a haberdashery with its own entrance. A delivery room was at the rear. There are six columns on the first story, topped by elaborate plaster decorations. A prismatic-glass clerestory windows surrounded the ground story. Within the basement, there was an arcade of glass display cases.
On the upper stories, the floors are made of wood. The ceilings are made of plaster applied onto lath and cloth, and the girders protrude into the surface of the ceiling. The large exterior windows illuminate the interior spaces and allow observers outside to see the girders on the ceiling. The mezzanine-level balcony, containing a curved glass railing, had toilets, telephones, parlors and drinking fountains. The main portion of the second floor was originally intended for womenswear and had natural oak furnishings and a terrazzo floor. The third floor was for millinery, bedding, wallpaper, drapery, and arts departments, and the fourth floor was initially reserved for future expansion. Both the third and fourth stories had oak floors. The rear annex had stockrooms, workrooms, and employee lockers and toilets on the second through fourth floors.
By the 1970s, the interior had been significantly modified to accommodate modern selling patterns. After the building became an apartment building in the 2000s, it was divided into 5 two-bedroom and 14 one-bedroom units on the second through fourth stories. Two of the single-bedroom apartments span two stories. The first floor contains 6,000 square feet (560 m2) of retail space. The interior was also renovated to incorporate a three-story atrium lit by a skylight.


== History ==

John Delbert Van Allen was a businessman who first worked for Field, Leiter & Company in Chicago, then A. T. Stewart Company and Morrison & Harriman in New York City. He worked in his employer's Chicago office from 1871 onward. In 1892, Van Allen and his family moved to Clinton, about 140 miles (230 km) west of Chicago. Van Allen became a business partner in a 2,500-square-foot (230 m2) dry-goods store at Second Street and Fifth Avenue South. The store acquired additional space in 1893 and 1897. The firm was renamed Van Allen & Son in 1905, upon which it expanded again to 11,000 square feet (1,000 m2). The store's inventory expanded in the late 1900s to encompass a variety of clothing styles, and by 1908 the store was earning about $300,000 annually. At the end of the next year, Van Allen bought the store's site.


=== Development ===


==== Planning ====
Van Allen was ready to build a new store by September 1910. By then, the Peoples Savings Bank in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, was under construction; Frederick Shaver, the bank's president, recommended that Van Allen hire Sullivan to design the new building. In a letter to Van Allen dated September 20, 1910, Shaver mentioned Sullivan's Transportation Building at the 1893 World Columbian Exposition, the Auditorium Hotel, and the Carson's building in Chicago, along with National Farmer's Bank of Owatonna, Minnesota, and wrote that Sullivan "designs buildings of great merit, beauty and simplicity". Sullivan invited Van Allen to Chicago to see the Carson's building the next month, though Van Allen's grandson, John B. Van Allen, later recalled that his grandfather may have already been aware of Sullivan's Chicago work, especially the Carson's building.
The early evolution of the building plans is detailed in a series of letters exchanged between Sullivan and Van Allen; the Art Institute of Chicago has collected 110 letters from Sullivan and 7 letters from Van Allen on the topic. By March 1911, Van Allen had formally offered the job to Sullivan, and on March 23 of that year, Sullivan sent the entrepreneur a rough sketch of the new store's first floor. The Van Allen site included a section that extended north from the lot's northwestern corner. To take advantage of this northern extension, Sullivan placed the entrance on the south, facing Fifth Avenue, and divided the floor plan into four north–south aisles. The aisles were 21 feet (6.4 m) wide, which Van Allen believed was too narrow, so Sullivan prepared revised plans for a three-aisle layout at Van Allen's request. Sullivan's draftsman Homer Sailor assisted with the drawings. In January 1912, Sullivan sent Van Allen revised plans for "a simple quiet building; yet with an air of distinction that comes from knowing how to do it". These plans called for a building with metal-trimmed openings; a light terracotta facade (used at Van Allen's request); and open-plan interiors.
To save money, Van Allen proposed sharing a party wall with a neighboring Woolworth store building to the west; this plan was too complex to actually implement, and the two businesses ultimately built separate party walls. Sullivan and Van Allen also discussed using light-colored brick rather than terracotta; they ultimately decided on darker brick. On April 3, 1912, Sullivan wrote to Van Allen stating, "My feeling is moving away from white enamelled terra cotta into a conception of brick and terra cotta in soft low tones." Plans for the Van Allen Building were filed that month, at which point it was expected to cost $100,000. In August 1912, the Van Allen firm acquired the nearby Reid-Dewitt building as a temporary store location. By then, plans had been drawn up for a brick structure with stone trim. The following month, Van Allen moved to the temporary store, allowing the existing site to be cleared. Material and design specifications continued to be tweaked through late 1912, at which point Van Allen was impatient to start construction.


==== Construction ====

A local resident, Dan Haring, was hired as the structure's general contractor. The Price Brick Yard was the brick contractor, and Clinton Bridge Works was the steel contractor. Workers discovered quicksand while excavating test pits into the site. According to one account, after this happened, Sullivan would sit on a keg of nails across the street and direct work on the building when it was under construction. Excavation work began on May 1, 1913, and attracted many passersby. By mid-May, the excavation work was nearly completed, and foundations were being installed.
Haring began work on the superstructure immediately after the site had been cleared.  The initial delivery of steelwork was sufficient for the first and second stories, though steel deliveries were delayed until late August and early September. Two derricks were installed to erect the beams. The steel frame had progressed to the top of the first floor by September 26 and the third floor by October 17. The steelwork was completed by November 14, followed by the walls, which were completed by December 20.  The scaffolding was removed in May 1914, and the public saw the facade for the first time. That September, the Van Allen firm acquired Frank Moses's decorative arts firm.


=== Use as department store ===


==== Van Allen Department Store ====
The new Van Allen Building formally opened the week of September 29, 1914, and was completed in early 1915. It was, at the time, the only multi-story store in Clinton. Sources disagree on whether the building remained within its $100,000 budget or whether its budget had increased to $126,226. When the store opened, it hosted weekly musical performances. During World War I, the American Red Cross moved into the first floor. The Red Cross facility opened in February 1917 and outgrew its space within a month; by the end of the year, two rooms were set aside for hospital supplies and surgical dressing. The fourth floor also had Red Cross workrooms. By the early 1920s, the store had a mail order department, and it employed a personal shopper. Advertising campaigns in local newspapers attracted customers from across rural Iowa.
A millinery department was added in 1924 as part of a renovation. In 1926, the firm opened 8,000 square feet (740 m2) of sales space in the basement, with separate family, children's, ready-to-wear, outdoor, and domestic goods departments. The Folwell Crockery company also moved into the building. The next year, Van Allen & Son announced that it would add several departments to the second floor, while the third floor would become a women's ready-to-wear department. This work was completed by 1928; the fourth floor had a wallpaper department, in addition to the second- and third-story departments. After Van Allen died in 1929, his family continued operating the store, and they announced plans the next year to expand the business into additional departments.  Although the store began operating one fewer day per week in the 1930s, business remained steady. During the Christmas and holiday season, Van Allen & Son decorated the store elaborately, with a Santa replica and a Christmas star.
In 1940, the company remodeled the building's Second Street display windows and removed the private haberdashery entrance. Van Allen & Son also rebuilt the entrance vestibules and added an elevator. Business at the store prospered during World War II, despite downturns elsewhere.  John D. Van Allen's son, Fred, operated the store until his own death in 1953; his son John B. took over as the store's president. Over the years, maintenance became more difficult because Sullivan had chosen different materials for each of his Iowa buildings, many of which were no longer widely used by the late 20th century. For example, a fire damaged the facade in 1958, after which Van Allen & Son had to reuse bricks from one of the side elevations.


==== Petersen's store ====

Petersen-Harned-Von Maur, a department store in Davenport, Iowa, acquired the Van Allen company in 1968; this was Petersen's first branch store outside its flagship in Davenport. At the time, the Van Allen Building employed 100 people, who continued to be employed by Petersen's. The building continued to be owned by John B. Van Allen, who leased it to Petersen's. John B. became the store's manager, and the building retained the Van Allen name, though Petersen's considered renovating the structure after acquiring the store. Phil Feddersen, a local architect, renovated the building in 1976. This work included adding glass-and-mahogany doors, and replacing the original upper-story windows with bronze-tinted windows.
The Van Allen Building was designated as a National Historic Landmark in January 1976, in large part because it was one of the best-preserved surviving examples of Sullivan's later work. The landmark designation was announced before John Van Allen had had the chance to review the official nomination form, but both Van Allen and Petersen's officials supported the designation. At the time, it was one of 14 National Historic Landmarks in Iowa. The designation made the building eligible for federal matching funds for preservation, as well as tax credits and some demolition protections.
Petersen's operated the store until it announced in March 1987 that the Clinton store would close; at the time, the company wished to focus on operating single-level stores. At that point, the store had only 50 employees, and the company had shuttered all of its downtown locations in other cities. This was part of a trend where large department stores across the US were moving away from downtowns into shopping malls. Petersen's listed the Van Allen Building for sale that April at about $250,000, and it began contacting department stores nationwide to gauge their interest in the building. The Van Allen Building closed on May 2, 1987, and the building then sat unused. Local merchants expressed concerns that the closure would negatively impact business in downtown Clinton. Van Allen wished to sell the building, but did not exclude the possibility of demolishing it; as one city councilman later said, such a demolition might have led to the destruction of other buildings in downtown Clinton.


=== Later usage ===


==== Initial renovation ====
Crombie Taylor, a retired University of Southern California dean, led efforts to restore the building; he had previously renovated some of Sullivan's other designs. After learning in early 1988 that the structure had been vacant for a year, Taylor moved to Clinton and formed the Van Allen Foundation to help save the structure. The foundation sought to convert the building into a museum and cultural center, with exhibits about Sullivan's work at ground level and offices for historical organizations on the upper floors. The architect Gyo Obata became chairman of the foundation's board, and the architect John Vinci also joined the restoration effort. The Van Allen Foundation turned on the heat to prevent the building from decaying further, and it obtained an option to buy the building in 1989.
The foundation received a $80,000 state grant in March 1990 to help purchase the building, and it appointed a steering committee the next month to raise money for restoration. The Clinton City Council purchased the Van Allen Building for $250,000 that May. The building was then leased to the Van Allen Foundation for 25 years. At the time, the terracotta alone was valued at $750,000, far higher than the purchase price. After the city purchased the building, the Van Allen Foundation renovated the ground floor and repainted exterior decorations. The project was funded by $105,000 from the Iowa government and $200,000 in private donations; the Clinton County government also provided an $8,000 grant. Taylor invited preservationists and architects to visit Clinton and convince community groups to use the structure, and the foundation allowed donors to sponsor 1-square-foot (0.093 m2) increments of the building.
The ground floor reopened on October 6, 1991. Initially, the ground floor had a photography exhibit on Sullivan's work and another exhibit about the building's history, and some space was rented out for public use. Later that year, the foundation requested another $25,000 from the city for repairs. Taylor believed that the building, once fully restored, would become a visitor attraction in a similar fashion to the Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio in Oak Park, Illinois. He anticipated raising money through merchandise sales. The foundation recorded 5,000 visitors in its first five months of the building's reopening. The town's mayor at the time said that Taylor had "tugged and pulled and charmed our citizens into a cadre of strong supporters".


==== Search for an alternate use ====
The Van Allen Foundation sought another $250,000–500,000 to renovate the upper floors, and it wished to restore the store's original appearance. It enlisted college students for the restoration process. Taylor, who wanted to preserve the Van Allen Building as an architectural history center, denied many requests to host activities there, which slowly led to community members avoiding it; he resigned as the foundation's director in 1993. The foundation struggled to fundraise, and after its expenses began to surpass income, the foundation's director Indra Brewer agreed to stop taking a salary in 1994. The next year, the Van Allen Foundation began interviewing cultural groups within 50 miles (80 km) of Clinton to gauge their interest in using the building. The foundation also hired a consultant to consider alternate uses for the building. In late 1995, the city council voted against either selling the structure or appointing a task force to discuss the building's future uses, though Clinton mayor Darrell Smith did eventually appoint a task force.

The attempts to reuse the building had stalled by 1996 after proposals to convert it into a theater, an art center, or a museum all failed. Exacerbating the Van Allen Foundation's financial issues, a boiler malfunction that February caused a water pipe leak that damaged large parts of the building. Following the pipe burst, the Van Allen Task Force requested that the city council allocate $99,000 for repairs. At the time, the history museum was closed, but the building still hosted events such as an antique market, a car show, auctions, and theatrical performances. There were also proposals to convert the building into an aerospace museum or a Clinton School Board office. Due to continued financial issues, the Van Allen Foundation moved out of the building in July 1996; all the utility services were shut off, though cursory inspections at the time did not reveal any structural issues. The Clinton City Council voted in January 1997 to place the building for sale.
The city council received three proposals in late 1997, which variously envisioned converting the building into a restaurant and entertainment center, a retail store, or low-income housing. The council did not endorse any of the proposals, instead soliciting more bids. In October 1999, Heartland Properties of Wisconsin and Community Housing Initiatives (CHI) of Iowa proposed converting the ground story into commercial office space and the upper stories into 19 apartments for about $2.1 million. The proposal was contingent on the city council's approval of a Self-Supported Municipal Improvement District allowing local businesses to fund improvements in downtown Clinton, which was approved later that month. The city council approved plans in November 1999 to resell the Van Allen Building to Heartlan

pages.title: Louis Sullivan
pages.text:
Louis Henry Sullivan (September 3, 1856 – April 14, 1924) was an American architect, and has been called a "father of skyscrapers" and "father of modernism". He was an influential architect of the Chicago School, a mentor to Frank Lloyd Wright, and an inspiration to the Chicago group of architects who have come to be known as the Prairie School. Along with Wright and Henry Hobson Richardson, Sullivan is one of "the recognized trinity of American architecture." The phrase "form follows function" is attributed to him; it encapsulated earlier theories of architecture and he applied them to the modern age of the skyscraper. In 1944, Sullivan was the second architect to posthumously receive the AIA Gold Medal.


== Early life and career ==
Sullivan was born to a Swiss-born mother, Andrienne née  List (who had emigrated to Boston from Geneva with her parents and two siblings, Jenny, b. 1836, and Jules, b. 1841) and an Irish-born father, Patrick Sullivan. Both had immigrated to the United States in the late 1840s. He learned that he could both graduate from high school a year early and bypass the first two years at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology by passing a series of examinations. Entering MIT at the age of sixteen, Sullivan studied architecture there briefly. After one year of study, he moved to Philadelphia and took a job with architect Frank Furness.
The Depression of 1873 dried up much of Furness's work, and he was forced to let Sullivan go. Sullivan moved to Chicago in 1873 to take part in the building boom following the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. He worked for William LeBaron Jenney, the architect often credited with erecting the first steel frame building. After less than a year with Jenney, Sullivan moved to Paris and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts for a year. He returned to Chicago and began work for the firm of Joseph S. Johnston & John Edelman as a draftsman. Johnston & Edleman were commissioned for the design of the Moody Tabernacle, and tasked Sullivan with the design of the interior decorative fresco secco stencils (stencil technique applied on dry plaster). In 1879 Dankmar Adler hired Sullivan. A year later, Sullivan became a partner in Adler's firm. The time at Adler & Sullivan marked the beginning of Sullivan's most productive years.
Adler and Sullivan initially achieved fame as theater architects. While most of their theaters were in Chicago, their fame won commissions as far west as Pueblo, Colorado, and Seattle, Washington (unbuilt). The culminating project of this phase of the firm's history was the 1889 Auditorium Building (1886–90, opened in stages) in Chicago, an extraordinary mixed-use building that included not only a 4,200-seat theater, but also a hotel and an office building with a 17-story tower and commercial storefronts at the ground level of the building, fronting Congress and Wabash Avenues. After 1889 the firm became known for their office buildings, particularly the 1891 Wainwright Building in St. Louis and the Schiller (later Garrick) Building and theater (1890) in Chicago. Other buildings often noted include the Chicago Stock Exchange Building (1894), the Guaranty Building (also known as the Prudential Building) of 1895–96 in Buffalo, New York, and the 1899–1904 Carson Pirie Scott Department Store by Sullivan on State Street in Chicago.


== Sullivan and the steel high-rise ==

Prior to the late nineteenth century, the weight of a multi-story building had to be supported principally by the strength of its walls. The taller the building, the more strain is placed on the lower sections of the building; since there were clear engineering limits to the weight such "load-bearing" walls could sustain, tall designs meant massively thick walls on the ground floors, and definite limits on the building's height.
The development of cheap, versatile steel in the second half of the nineteenth century changed those rules. America was in the midst of rapid social and economic growth that made for great opportunities in architectural design. A much more urbanized society was forming and the society called out for new, larger buildings. The mass production of steel was the main driving force behind the ability to build skyscrapers during the mid-1880s. By assembling a framework of steel girders, architects and builders could create tall, slender buildings with a strong and relatively lightweight steel skeleton. The rest of the building elements—walls, floors, ceilings, and windows—were suspended from the skeleton, which carried the weight. This new way of constructing buildings, so-called "column-frame" construction, pushed them up rather than out. The steel weight-bearing frame allowed not just taller buildings, but permitted much larger windows, which meant more daylight reaching interior spaces. Interior walls became thinner, which created more usable (and rentable) floor space.
Chicago's Monadnock Building (not designed by Sullivan) straddles this remarkable moment of transition: the northern half of the building, finished in 1891, is of load-bearing construction, while the southern half, finished only two years later, is of column-frame construction. While experiments in this new technology were taking place in many cities, Chicago was the crucial laboratory. Industrial capital and civic pride drove a surge of new construction throughout the city's downtown in the wake of the 1871 fire.
The technical limits of weight-bearing masonry had formal and structural constraints which were remedied by Sullivan. None of the historical precedents were necessarily followed, causing a sort of literary, and technical crisis. Sullivan addressed the crisis by embracing the changes that came with the steel frame, creating a grammar of form for the high rise (base, shaft, and cornice), simplifying the appearance of the building by breaking away from historical styles, using his own intricate floral designs, in vertical bands, to draw the eye upward and to emphasize the vertical form of the building, and relating the shape of the building to its specific purpose. Such innovations were unique, and commercially successful.
In 1896, Louis Sullivan wrote:

It is the pervading law of all things organic and inorganic, of all things physical and metaphysical, of all things human, and all things super-human, of all true manifestations of the head, of the heart, of the soul, that the life is recognizable in its expression, that form ever follows function. This is the law. (italics in original)

"Form follows function" would become one of the prevailing tenets of modern architects.
Sullivan attributed the concept to Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect, engineer, and author, who first asserted in his book, De architectura (On architecture), that a structure must exhibit the three qualities of firmitas, utilitas, venustas – that is, it must be "solid, useful, beautiful." This credo, which placed the demands of practical use equal to aesthetics, later would be taken by influential designers to imply that decorative elements, which architects call "ornament", were superfluous in modern buildings, but Sullivan neither thought nor designed along such dogmatic lines during the peak of his career and this credo never put one concept above another. While his buildings could be spare and crisp in their principal masses, he often punctuated their plain surfaces with eruptions of lush Art Nouveau or Celtic Revival decorations, usually cast in iron or terra cotta, and ranging from organic forms, such as vines and ivy, to more geometric designs and interlace, inspired by his Irish design heritage. Terra cotta is lighter and easier to work with than stone masonry. Sullivan used it in his architecture because it had a malleability that was appropriate for his ornament. Probably the most famous example of ornament used by Sullivan is the writhing green ironwork that covers the entrance canopies of the Carson Pirie Scott store on south State Street.
Such ornaments, often executed by the younger draftsmen in Sullivan's employ, eventually would become Sullivan's trademark; to students of architecture, they are instantly recognizable as his signature.
Another signature element of Sullivan's work is the massive, semi-circular arch. Sullivan employed such arches throughout his career—in shaping entrances, in framing windows, or as interior design.
All of these elements are found in Sullivan's widely admired Guaranty Building, which he designed while partnered with Adler. Completed in 1895, this office building in Buffalo, New York is in the Palazzo style, visibly divided into three "zones" of design: a plain, wide-windowed base for the ground-level shops; the main office block, with vertical ribbons of masonry rising unimpeded across nine upper floors to emphasize the building's height; and an ornamented cornice perforated by round windows at the roof level, where the building's mechanical units (such as the elevator motors) were housed. The cornice is covered by Sullivan's trademark Art Nouveau vines and each ground-floor entrance is topped by a semi-circular arch.
Because Sullivan's remarkable accomplishments in design and construction occurred at such a critical time in architectural history, he often has been described as the "father" of the American skyscraper. But many architects had been building skyscrapers before or as contemporaries of Sullivan; they were designed as an expression of new technology. Chicago was replete with extraordinary designers and builders in the late years of the nineteenth century, including Sullivan's partner, Dankmar Adler, as well as Daniel Burnham and John Wellborn Root. Root was one of the builders of the Monadnock Building (see above). That and another Root design, the Masonic Temple Tower (both in Chicago), are cited by many as the originators of skyscraper aesthetics of bearing wall and column-frame construction, respectively.


== Later career and decline ==

In 1890, Sullivan was one of the ten U.S. architects, five from the east and five from the west, chosen to build a major structure for the "White City", the World's Columbian Exposition, held in Chicago in 1893. Sullivan's massive Transportation Building and huge arched "Golden Door" stood out as the only building not of the current Beaux-Arts style, and with the only multicolored facade in the entire White City. Sullivan and fair director Daniel Burnham were vocal about their displeasure with each other. Sullivan later claimed (1922) that the fair set the course of American architecture back "for half a century from its date, if not longer." His was the only building to receive extensive recognition outside America, receiving three medals from the French-based Union Centrale des Arts Decoratifs the following year.
Like all American architects, Adler and Sullivan suffered a precipitous decline in their practice with the onset of the Panic of 1893. According to Charles Bebb, who was working in the office at that time, Adler borrowed money to try to keep employees on the payroll. By 1894, however, in the face of continuing financial distress with no relief in sight, Adler and Sullivan dissolved their partnership. The Guaranty Building was considered the last major project of the firm.
By both temperament and connections, Adler had been the one who brought in new business to the partnership, and following the rupture Sullivan received few large commissions after the Carson Pirie Scott Department Store. He went into a twenty-year-long financial and emotional decline, beset by a shortage of commissions, chronic financial problems, and alcoholism. He obtained a few commissions for small-town Midwestern banks (see below), wrote books, and in 1922 appeared as a critic of Raymond Hood's winning entry for the Tribune Tower competition.
In 1922, Sullivan was paid $100 a month to write an autobiography in installments to be published in the journal for the American Institute of Architects. Sullivan worked on the series with Journal editor Charles Harris Whitaker, who advised he "plot out the material by periods." The Autobiography of an Idea began its publication in the June 1922 Journal for the American Institute of Architects and upon its conclusion was published as a book.
He died in a Chicago hotel room on April 14, 1924. He left a wife, Mary Azona Hattabaugh, from whom he was separated. A modest headstone marks his final resting spot in Graceland Cemetery in Chicago's Uptown and Lake View neighborhood. Later, a monument was erected in Sullivan's honor, a few feet from his headstone.


== Legacy ==
Sullivan's legacy is contradictory. Some consider him the first modernist. His forward-looking designs clearly anticipate some issues and solutions of Modernism; however, his embrace of ornament makes his contribution distinct from the Modern Movement that coalesced in the 1920s and became known as the "International Style". Sullivan's built work expresses the appeal of his incredible designs: the vertical bands on the Wainwright Building, the burst of welcoming Art Nouveau ironwork on the corner entrance of the Carson Pirie Scott store, the (lost) terra cotta griffins and porthole windows on the Union Trust building, and the white angels of the Bayard Building, Sullivan's only work in New York City. Except for some designs by his longtime draftsman George Grant Elmslie, and the occasional tribute to Sullivan such as Schmidt, Garden & Martin's First National Bank in Pueblo, Colorado (built across the street from Adler and Sullivan's Pueblo Opera House), his style is unique. A visit to the preserved Chicago Stock Exchange trading floor, now at The Art Institute of Chicago, is proof of the immediate and visceral power of the ornament that he used so selectively.
After his death Sullivan was referred to as a bold architect: "Boldly he challenged the whole theory of copying and imitating, and the catchword of "precedent", declaring that architecture was naturally a living and creative art." James Marston Fitch wrote that Sullivan "was quick to see the advantages in other men's work, and quick to adapt them to his own uses . . . He was a man in search of an architectural idiom which would be, not his own personal property, but that of the American people."  Sullivan believed that architecture was a manifestation of a culture, its people, its needs, and its values. The architect, Sullivan told the Chicago Architectural Club in 1899, "is and imperatively shall be an interpreter of the national life of his time."
Original drawings and other archival materials from Sullivan are held by the Ryerson & Burnham Libraries in the Art Institute of Chicago and by the drawings and archives department in the Avery Architectural and Fine Arts Library at Columbia University. Fragments of Sullivan buildings also are held in many fine art and design museums around the world.


== Preservation ==
During the postwar era of urban renewal, Sullivan's works fell into disfavor, and many were demolished. In the 1970s, growing public concern for these buildings finally resulted in many being saved. The most vocal voice was Richard Nickel, who organized protests against the demolition of architecturally significant buildings. Nickel and others sometimes rescued decorative elements from condemned buildings, sneaking in during demolition. Nickel died inside Sullivan's Stock Exchange building while trying to retrieve some elements, when a floor above him collapsed. Nickel had compiled extensive research on Adler and Sullivan and their many architectural commissions, which he intended to publish in book form.
After Nickel's death, in 1972, the Richard Nickel Committee was formed, to arrange for completion of his book, which was published in 2010. The book features all 256 commissions of Adler and Sullivan. The extensive archive of photographs and research that underpinned the book was donated to the Ryerson and Burnham Libraries at The Art Institute of Chicago. More than 1,300 photographs may be viewed on their website and more than 15,000 photographs are part of the collection at The Art Institute of Chicago. As finally published, the book, The Complete Architecture of Adler & Sullivan, was authored by Richard Nickel, Aaron Siskind, John Vinci, and Ward Miller.

Another champion of Sullivan's legacy was the architect Crombie Taylor (1907–1991), of Crombie Taylor Associates. After working in Chicago, where he headed the famous "Institute of Design" (later known as the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT)) in the 1950s and early 1960s, he moved to Southern California. He led the effort to save the Van Allen Building in Clinton, Iowa from demolition. Taylor, acting as an aesthetic consultant, worked on the renovation of the Auditorium Building (now Roosevelt University) in Chicago.
When he read an article about the planned demolition in Clinton, he uprooted his family from their home in southern California and moved them to Iowa. With the vision of a destination neighborhood comparable to Oak Park, Illinois, he set about creating a nonprofit to save the building, and was successful in doing so. Another advocate for the buildings of both Sullivan and Wright was Jack Randall, who led an effort to save the Wainwright Building in St. Louis, Missouri at a very critical time. He relocated his family to Buffalo, New York to save Sullivan's Guaranty Building and Frank Lloyd Wright's Darwin Martin House from possible demolition. His efforts were successful in both St. Louis and Buffalo.
A collection of architectural ornaments designed by Sullivan is on permanent display at Lovejoy Library at Southern Illinois University Edwardsville. The St. Louis Art Museum also has Sullivan architectural elements displayed. The City Museum in St. Louis has a large collection of Sullivan ornamentation on display, including a cornice from the demolished Chicago Stock Exchange, 29 feet long on one side, 13 feet on another, and nine feet high.
The Guaranty Building Interpretive Center in Buffalo, on the first floor of the building now owned and occupied by the law firm Hodgson Russ, LLP, opened in 2017. The exhibit space was financed by Hodgson Russ and co-designed by Flynn Battaglia Architects and Hadley Exhibits. It features a scale model of the building by David J. Carli, professor of engineering at the State University of New York at Alfred. The center's exhibits were donated to Preservation Buffalo Niagara. The center, the only museum dedicated to Sullivan, is open to the public.


== Sullivan in Ayn Rand's The Fountainhead ==
That the fictional character of Henry Cameron in Ayn Rand's 1943 novel The Fountainhead was similar to the real-life Sullivan was noted, if only in passing, by at least one journalist contemporary to the book.
Although Rand's journal notes contain in toto only some 50 lines directly referring to Sullivan, it is clear from her mention of Sullivan's Autobiography of an Idea (1924) in her 25th-anniversary introduction to her earlier novel We the Living (first published in 1936, and unrelated to architecture) that she was intimately familiar with his life and career. The term "the Fountainhead", which appears nowhere in Rand's novel proper, is found twice (as "the fountainhead" and later as "the fountain head") in Sullivan's autobiography, both times used metaphorically.
The fictional Cameron is, like Sullivan – whose physical description he matches – a great innovative skyscraper pioneer late in the nineteenth century who dies impoverished and embittered in the mid-1920s. Cameron's rapid decline is explicitly attributed to the wave of classical Greco-Roman revivalism in architecture in the wake of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, just as Sullivan in his autobiography attributed his own downfall to the same event.
The major difference between novel and real life was in the chronology of Cameron's relation with his protégé Howard Roark, the novel's hero, who eventually goes on to redeem his vision. That Roark's uncompromising individualism and his innovative organic style in architecture were drawn from the life and work of Frank Lloyd Wright is clear from Rand's journal notes, her correspondence, and various contemporary accounts. In the novel, however, the 23-year-old Roark, a generation younger than the real-life Wright, becomes Cameron's protégé in the early 1920s, when Sullivan was long in decline.
The young Wright, by contrast, was Sullivan's protégé for seven years, beginning in 1887, when Sullivan was at the height of his fame and power. The two architects would sever their ties in 1894 due to Sullivan's angry reaction to Wright's moonlighting in breach of his contract with Sullivan, but Wright continued to call Sullivan "lieber Meister" ("beloved Master") for the rest of his life. After decades of estrangement, Wright would again become close to the now-destitute Sullivan in the early 1920s, the time when Roark first comes under the likewise impoverished Cameron's tutelage in the novel. Wright, however, was now in his fifties. Nevertheless, both the young Roark and middle-aged Wright had in common at that time that they both faced a decade of struggle ahead. After the triumphs earlier in his career, Wright came increasingly to be viewed as a has-been, until he experienced a renaissance in the latter half of the 1930s with such projects as Fallingwater and the Johnson Wax Headquarters.

=== Banks ===

Sulliven's later output consisted primarily of a series of small bank and commercial buildings in the Midwest. When the director of a bank that was considering hiring him asked Sullivan why they should engage him at a cost higher than the bids received for a conventional Neo-Classic styled building from other architects, Sullivan is reported to have replied, "A thousand architects could design those buildings. Only I can design this one." He got the job. These commissions are collectively referred to as Sullivan's "Jewel Boxes", and all still stand.

Peoples Savings Bank, Cedar Rapids, Iowa (1912)
Henry Adams Building, Algona, Iowa (1913)
